News 2 d ago No more flights to Prague or Berlin: which destinations are cut from airBalticâs schedule News 2026.08.22 10:00 âI think in Lithuanianâ: the Azerbaijani girl who aced the Lithuanian national exam AM Aida MurauskaitÄ, LRT.lt 2026.08.22 10:00 Zeinab Mamedova | Personal album When Zeinab Mamedova arrived in Lithuania at the age of nine, she spoke no Lithuanian whatsoever. Within a few months, she was fluent. This summer, she scored 100% on Lithuania's school-leaving Lithuanian language and literature exam âÂ and won a place to study medicine.Â Zeinab was born in Almaty, Kazakhstan's largest city, to an Azerbaijani family. Her first language is Russian, the dominant language of Almaty; she also speaks Azerbaijani. Lithuanian was acquired in a classroom, in the small northeastern Lithuanian town of Utena, where she moved with her mother in November 2015. "I didn't know anything about Lithuania," she recalls. "A few days after we arrived, I started school." Learning by pointing The school her family chose â KraÅ¡uona middle school â had a teacher experienced in working with children who spoke little or no Lithuanian. This was a practical consideration, since nine-year-old Zeinab understood nothing of what was said around her, except in maths lessons. But she was, by her own account, unbothered. "I was a child, so I didn't really worry about it. I just wanted to make friends. And since none of the other children spoke English or Russian, we tried to communicate in Lithuanian. My classmates taught me words â they'd hold up a pencil and say 'pieÅ¡tukas'. That's how the language slowly stuck." Her very first Lithuanian word, she says, was 'pienas' â milk â learned before she left Kazakhstan, from her stepfather, an Azerbaijani man living in Lithuania. "I didn't even know where Lithuania was at that point. But I asked him how to say 'milk'." Zeinab Mamedova | Personal album She found Lithuanian difficult at first, particularly its complex system of grammatical case endings â Lithuanian is one of the most grammatically intricate languages in Europe, with seven noun cases. "I never liked the locative case," she says, referring to a grammar case that turns the noun into a location. "At home I'd guess at how words should sound. But eventually it just settled in. Lithuanian became very beautiful to me." Reading helped. Zeinab had been a keen reader since childhood, and worked her way through Lithuanian books as her vocabulary expanded. But Zeinab herself believes communicating with others in Lithuanian was most helpful in learning the language. By the time she returned to school after her first summer holiday, she was speaking fluently and without an accent. Her speech therapist, who had been assigned to help her when she first arrived, was astonished. "She told me: 'I think you're very bright, you should become a doctor. My daughter got into medicine, and Lithuania needs good doctors.'" Zeinab laughed it off at the time, saying she would never pick medicine. Ten years later, she changed her mind. "I couldn't let myself celebrate" Scoring 100% on a national language exam is unusual enough for native speakers. For someone who arrived in the country speaking none of it, it is remarkable. Zeinab Mamedova at the ceremony honouring school-graduates who scored 100% in Utena | Utena district municipality Lithuania's school-leaving exams â taken at the end of secondary school, roughly equivalent to A-levels in the UK â are graded on a national scale, with Lithuanian language and literature among the most demanding. Zeinab sat five exams in total: Lithuanian, history, biology, chemistry and mathematics, plus an earlier international English qualification. Her results across all of them were high enough to secure a place at the Lithuanian University of Health Sciences in Kaunas. But the Lithuanian result came at a cost. The exam requires a written essay based on readings drawn at random from a mandatory syllabus, meaning candidates have no way of knowing in advance which texts will come up, and must work through the entire list for the best result. "In years 11 and 12, I didn't really live a normal life â I mostly just studied. I read every book on the syllabus. I watched every documentary. Even when I was eating, exercising, just walking around, I'd listen to audiobooks. I wanted to go into the exam knowing I'd have something to write about, whatever the question." She even skipped her high school's end-of-year farewell ceremony â a significant occasion in Lithuanian school culture â because the Lithuanian exam was two days later. "I couldn't let myself celebrate, knowing the exam was coming," she said. Zeinab Mamedova | Personal album Though initially hoping to get 100% due to her love for literature, after sitting the paper, she was convinced she'd done badly, and rang her teacher in distress. "She wrote to comfort me. That night I barely slept," Zeinab recalls. When results day came, she was visiting her father and grandparents in Kazakhstan. The results system initially wouldn't load â something she attributes to accessing it from abroad. "After 15 minutes it finally opened and I saw 100. I couldn't believe it. I started screaming, grabbed everyone around me, and said: 'That's it. Thank God.'" "I think in Lithuanian" Zeinab's family speaks several languages at home â Azerbaijani, Russian and Lithuanian. When her younger brothers were born, the family made a deliberate shift. "We wanted them to learn Lithuanian well, so we started speaking Lithuanian at home too. My mum doesn't really speak it, but she understands a lot." She is matter-of-fact about where her sense of identity now sits. "I think in Lithuanian," she says. "Ten years ago I would never have imagined things would turn out this way. When I arrived as a small child, my mum was even worried I might not learn the language and we'd have to move to Vilnius and put me in a Russian-language school. I'm very glad that didn't happen." She is considering specialising in gynaecology â the field she associates most closely with life itself, she says â though nothing is fixed yet. One last trip to the mountains LRT.lt spoke to Zeinab on the last day of her summer visit to Kazakhstan, as she was preparing to return to Lithuania and move to Kaunas, a city she barely knows, to begin her degree. Zeinab Mamedova in Kazachstan | Personal album That morning, she and her grandmother had driven to the mountains outside Almaty. "We are mountain people. Even though we live in Kazakhstan, we are Azerbaijani, and Azerbaijan is deeply connected to the Caucasus mountains. Mountains have always been part of our culture. If we have nothing to do, we just get in the car and drive up." One of the biggest differences between her old life and her new one, she says, is simply the landscape: Lithuania is flat. "When I first arrived, that felt very strange." She will miss Kazakhstan, she admits â but she already misses Lithuania more. "I miss Utena. I miss home." Starting university in an unfamiliar city, she says, feels both daunting and overdue. "School is behind me now. Twelve years is a very long time. I'm ready for something new." The short version is Lithuania. The longer story begins when she moved to Northern Ireland at age 5, where she spent most of her childhood and teenage years, before moving to Croatia to study at university. This story is based on a press release from Kaunas University of Technology This summer, however, KaniauskaitÄ returned to Lithuania for several months, taking an internship at Kaunas University of Technology while experiencing something she had never done before: living independently in the country she has always considered home. âI have always considered myself Lithuanian and, although I have spent most of my life in Northern Ireland, I still feel closer to Lithuania,â she said. Growing up between cultures At home in Northern Ireland, Lithuanian culture remained a constant. Her family spoke Lithuanian, listened to Lithuanian music and lived near other Lithuanian families. Lithuanian food was served at home, while Christmas and Easter were celebrated with traditional dishes. Outside the home, KaniauskaitÄ became part of Northern Irish life, celebrating Halloween, Valentineâs Day and local holidays with friends. âThere was quite a clear divide between the culture at home and the culture outside it, and I was part of both,â she said. Balancing the two cultures was not always easy. As a child, she was eager to fit into Northern Irish society, while her mother worked to ensure that Lithuanian traditions remained part of her life. âIâm grateful to her for that now,â KaniauskaitÄ said. She also found herself sometimes feeling like an outsider, although friendships with local people and people from other backgrounds helped her navigate those differences. âNorthern Ireland is very diverse, so living there taught me to be more open-minded,â she said. âGrowing up among people from different backgrounds taught me to understand and accept others, and that has become an important part of how I see the world.â A move to Croatia When it came time for university, KaniauskaitÄ chose Croatia, where she is studying digital marketing in Zagreb. Her decision had a personal side, too: Her boyfriend, Filip, lives there. The couple have been together for almost six years, including four years in a long-distance relationship before she began university. They have spent the past two years living together in Croatia. Living in Zagreb has given her another culture against which to compare Lithuania and Northern Ireland. She says Lithuanians can sometimes appear reserved and distant, while Croatians tend to be warmer and more openly sociable. Neither approach, she emphasises, is necessarily better. Zagreb, Croatia | Shutterstock âAs someone who values personal space, I feel comfortable with Lithuanian culture,â she said. âLithuanians can sometimes come across as cold, but you generally know where you stand with them.â Croatia, meanwhile, has taught her to slow down. Growing up in a small town in Northern Ireland, she was accustomed to a quieter environment. Zagreb, with a population of about 800,000, initially surprised her with its noise and fast pace. When she returns to Lithuania, she appreciates the quiet streets, orderly traffic and greenery. âLithuania, to me, is first and foremost about family and nature â enjoying what surrounds you and appreciating what you have,â she said. Returning to Lithuania Her decision to spend the summer in Lithuania was about more than gaining professional experience. KaniauskaitÄ wanted to spend more time with relatives and immerse herself more deeply in a culture she had maintained from abroad but had never experienced as an independent adult. âThere is a lot of uncertainty about my future, and I realise that the time I can spend with my family in Lithuania is limited,â she said. She also wanted to test her own ability to live in Lithuania. Sofija KaniauskaitÄ | KTU Although she speaks Lithuanian fluently, she said she is not always confident in her language skills. Living and working in the country gave her an opportunity to challenge herself. She chose an internship in the International Relations Department at Kaunas University of Technology because her own experience of moving between countries gave her an understanding of the challenges international students can face. âI wanted to help other students facing difficulties similar to those I have experienced myself,â she said. During the internship, she has worked mainly with international students, managing an email inbox, answering questions about applications and helping resolve problems. She also interviewed students online and helped welcome and coordinate new arrivals during Welcome Week. Having moved countries twice herself, KaniauskaitÄ says she can easily relate to students adjusting to a new environment. Her own social circle reflects that international experience. In both Lithuania and Croatia, many of her friends are international students rather than locals. âMeeting and communicating with different people helps me become more open to new connections,â she said. KTU - Kauno technologijos universitetas | V. Raupelio / LRT nuotr. Feeling Lithuanian Perhaps the most important part of her time in Kaunas has been something much simpler: speaking Lithuanian every day. For years, her visits to Lithuania had been limited largely to summer holidays with relatives. This time, she experienced ordinary life in the country â working, living independently and constantly surrounded by the Lithuanian language. âBeing able to speak my native language every day helped me feel more Lithuanian,â she said. âWhen Iâm here, I have absolutely no doubt that I am Lithuanian.â She has also noticed qualities in Lithuanians that remind her of herself. She describes Lithuanians as logical and direct, with a strong preference for clarity and doing things properly. Growing up, she was often told she was the same way. âIt feels special to recognise these similarities between myself and other Lithuanians, even though I havenât lived in Lithuania for a long time,â she said. Kaunas, LaisvÄs alÄja | J. StaceviÄiaus / LRT nuotr. Finding her place in Kaunas Before arriving in Kaunas, KaniauskaitÄ knew little about the city. She had heard Lithuanians say there was not much to do there and arrived without particularly high expectations. Several months later, her view has changed. âWhat I appreciate most about Kaunas is its calm atmosphere and nature, but calm certainly does not mean boring,â she said. âThe city is lively and there is plenty to do â you just have to look for it.â For her, the appeal lies in the balance between city life and nature. âYou can feel the rhythm of the city while still being able to escape into nature, relax and slow down for a while,â she said. Kaunas | Shutterstock Kaunas has gradually become more than a temporary home for an internship. The experience has strengthened her desire to return to Lithuania someday, whether to study, work or live. That decision, however, can wait. KaniauskaitÄ has one more year of her bachelorâs degree in Croatia before she plans to pursue a masterâs degree. She has not yet decided where. âI enjoy living in both Croatia and Lithuania, so ideally I would like both countries to be part of my life,â she said. For now, she does not feel pressure to choose one country over the other. Living in different places, she says, is a privilege â and she remains open to adding more countries to the story. âI would like to continue having experiences like these in the future â perhaps not only in Lithuania or Croatia, but in other countries too,â she said. âMy future is still very uncertain, so time will tell where this journey eventually takes me.â LRT English Newsletter Every Friday morning. https://www.aol.co.uk/articles/thomas-tu.text: Tashan Deniran-Alleyne Sun, September 27, 2026 at 1:28 PM UTC 0 Thomas Tuchel has revealed Lewis Hall missed some England training sessions with an injury scare, explaining the defender’s absence against Spain. Hall was an unused substitute as the Three Lions were beaten by the reigning world and European champions in their 2026/27 Nations League opener on Saturday evening . Instead, Nico O’Reilly played the full 90 minutes at Wembley Stadium and despite claiming the assist for Harry Kane’s goal to put England 2-1 up, the Manchester City youngster was at fault for Alex Baena’s equaliser and struggled to contain Lamine Yamal . By contrast, Hall was hailed for stifling the Spain winger when Newcastle faced Barcelona in the Champions League last season. To the surprise of some, Hall - who recently signed a new contract at St James’ Park - was not summoned from the bench against Spain , though Tuchel has provided the reason why. "He missed some training sessions with a bit of an injury scare, Lewis Hall,” the England boss told reporters. “That is why I was a bit hesitant to put him out there today. "He is an option, he trained well at the end of the week but he was out of training at the start, we didn't want to take any risk because there was high speed running to do and defending against Lamine Yamal. "I did not want to risk it. He is always in our discussions in the left-back position, he plays left-back at his club, Nico plays in centre midfield. "Lewis' situation is he will fight for his place and get his first matches, there are still a few matches to go." England are back in Nations League action on Tuesday evening as they face Czechia in Prague before rounding off the extended autumn international break against Croatia and the return meeting with Czechia. Bos , Worthy News Europe Bureau Chief WARSAW/BUDAPEST ( Worthy News ) – Polish police deployed officers to some 10,000 schools and other educational institutions Friday and detained ten people over threats of further violence after two knife attacks left a school employee dead and several others injured, authorities said. The nationwide security operation followed warnings circulating on social media about a supposed “Bloody Friday” campaign encouraging attacks on schools, prompting authorities to increase police patrols and investigate online threats. Several schools suspended classes as a precaution, particularly in the Mazovia region surrounding Warsaw, while police appealed to parents and teachers to report suspicious behavior. Don’t miss the stories Christians should be watching — subscribe to the Worthy Brief. The heightened security followed Thursday’s killing of a 37-year-old school caretaker at a primary school in Leszczydół-Nowiny, northeast of Warsaw. A 15-year-old former pupil allegedly attacked three employees with a knife, killing the woman and injuring the school’s principal and a teacher. Prime Minister Donald Tusk said the slain woman was a mother of two, while praising school employees who confronted the attacker despite the danger to their own lives. SECOND SCHOOL ATTACK The killing came a day after a 19-year-old vocational school student allegedly attacked people with a knife and other sharp weapons in Ostrołęka, northeastern Poland, injuring nine people before harming himself. The wounded included five students, two teachers and two bystanders. One teacher suffered serious injuries, although prosecutors said none of the victims’ lives remained in danger. Prosecutors said the suspect had also brought a backpack containing explosives into a classroom occupied by 11 people. The device did not detonate during the attack, but investigators later confirmed that it contained a powerful explosive charge. Both suspected attackers were detained. The 15-year-old was restrained by the school principal before police took him into custody, while the 19-year-old was arrested shortly after fleeing Wednesday’s attack. Prosecutors have charged the older suspect with multiple counts of attempted murder, but the younger teenager’s case is being handled by juvenile authorities. FEARS OF FURTHER VIOLENCE Tusk convened emergency talks with government ministers and senior security officials amid concerns that the attacks could inspire further violence. The prime minister said Thursday’s suspected attacker had worn a helmet-mounted camera, apparently intending to record the assault. Authorities had not established whether the attack was filmed. Police said the ten people detained Friday included a 13-year-old from Warsaw who allegedly posted a photograph of a knife in a classroom group chat and threatened fellow pupils. Officers also detained a 14-year-old carrying a knife and firecrackers at a Warsaw school, while two 15-year-olds near the capital were accused of posting a video containing death threats. In a separate case, a 17-year-old in Sierpc was detained Thursday after fellow students alerted a teacher to statements suggesting he was planning violence. Police found two knives in his possession. SCHOOLS CLOSE The incidents heightened concerns that online threats could inspire further attacks, although investigators had not established links between the two original school assaults. The growing concerns prompted authorities to suspend in-person classes in several districts, including Wyszków, Pułtusk and Ciechanów, while Warsaw authorities maintained normal teaching schedules with additional police patrols. Poland’s Central Bureau for Combating Cybercrime was investigating material circulating on the TikTok platform, including an account allegedly linked to Thursday’s attacker. However, Digital Affairs Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski said investigators had found no evidence of an organized nationwide campaign encouraging attacks. He warned that isolated individuals could still attempt to imitate the violence, even without evidence of a coordinated plot. SCHOOL VIOLENCE IN POLAND Authorities urged parents and teachers to remain vigilant and report credible threats while avoiding the spread of unverified claims online. Yet those warnings came too late for families affected by the attacks, particularly in Leszczydół-Nowiny, where the death of a school employee and mother of two has left a community mourning. Such violent attacks on schools remain relatively rare in Poland, a predominantly Roman Catholic nation, although previous incidents have also claimed lives. In May 2019, a 16-year-old pupil was stabbed to death by a fellow student at a Warsaw school, while another attack that month involving a firearm and an explosive device injured two people at a primary school in Brześć Kujawski.
